# aaSender — a HAAS-lookalike g-code sender for grblHAL / ClearCore

## Context

`/home/holla/aaSender` is empty apart from `images/haas1.jpg` and `images/haas2.jpg`,
photos of a classic (pre-NGC, green-screen) HAAS mill pendant. The goal is a
browser-based g-code sender whose entire operator interface replicates that
pendant, so students learning on HAAS machines can practice the real workflow —
modes, DISPLAY pages, HANDLE JOG, CYCLE START, offsets, on-control editing —
against a hobby-class grblHAL machine or nothing at all.

The target hardware is the companion project **`/home/holla/grblhal-clearcore`**
(Teknic ClearCore, SAME53, bare-metal grblHAL, 4-axis XYZA), which is already
bench-verified with Ethernet, telnet, WebSocket, HTTP, the WebUI plugin, SD job
streaming and USB CDC. It currently serves ESP3D-WebUI v3 from SD `/www`.
aaSender is the HAAS-skinned replacement for that UI.

**Decisions already made with the user:**
- Three transports: network WebSocket, Web Serial over USB, and a built-in
  simulator so a classroom seat needs no hardware.
- Full pendant replica — clickable keypad and green screen, operated like a real HAAS.
- Classic green-screen generation (the one in `images/`), not NGC.
- Scope: operator essentials **plus** programming — EDIT mode, MDI, offset entry.

### What the ClearCore project already settles

Read from `grblhal-clearcore/src/my_machine.h`, `src/webui/server.c` and `PLAN.md`:

| Fact | Consequence for aaSender |
|---|---|
| `ETHERNET/TELNET/WEBSOCKET/HTTP/WEBUI_ENABLE 1`, all bench-verified | WebSocket transport is available today, no firmware work |
| ESP3D-WebUI installs over the network: `GET /sdfiles?action=createdir&filename=www&path=/` then multipart-POST `index.html.gz` to `/sdfiles` | **Same install path for aaSender** — build to one gzipped file, no card removal |
| Board serves `/www/index.html.gz` at `/` | Served from the board ⇒ same origin ⇒ **no CORS problem at all** |
| USB CDC enumerates `2890:8022` | Web Serial transport works on the same board |
| `N_AXIS 4` (XYZA) | Position/offset pages are 4-axis, not 3 |
| `?` returns `<Idle\|MPos:0,0,0,0\|Bf:100,1023>` | RX buffer is **1023 bytes**, not the classic 128 — read it from `Bf:` |
| `N_TOOLS 0` in `src/grbl/config.h` | Board has **no tool table** — the sender must own it |
| `$397=250` needed for WebUI DRO push | Avoided: aaSender polls `?` itself, uniformly on all three transports |
| Repo is MIT; grblHAL core is GPLv3 | aaSender is a separate browser app, no grblHAL code linked — MIT is fine |

---

## Architecture

Vite + Preact, static build, no backend. Preact because ESP3D-WEBUI uses it (any
reference transfers), it is ~3 KB, and a pendant with ten display pages, a
program editor and live status needs real state management. Everything else is
stdlib or plain DOM.

The build must produce **one self-contained gzipped file** to sit on the board's
SD card next to where ESP3D-WebUI lives. `vite-plugin-singlefile` inlines JS/CSS
into `index.html`; a build step gzips it. Size budget: ESP3D-WebUI is 91 KB
gzipped, so **≤150 KB gzipped** is the target — checked in CI-ish fashion by a
line in the build script that fails loudly if it grows past that.

```
index.html
vite.config.js
src/
  main.jsx
  grbl.js          status/ok/error/alarm parsing, error+alarm tables,
                   character-counting job streamer
  transport.js     one interface, three impls: WebSocket | Web Serial | Simulator
  sim.js           virtual grblHAL machine (no hardware needed)
  haas.js          HAAS machine model: modes, work/tool offsets, timers,
                   grbl -> HAAS alarm mapping
  keys.js          pendant key table + key -> action dispatch
  ui/Pendant.jsx   bezel, logo, E-stop, handle-jog dial, keypad
  ui/Screen.jsx    green screen frame + DISPLAY page router
  ui/pages/*.jsx   Position, Program, Offset, CurrCmds, Alarms, Setng, ListProg, Help
  haas.css         green-screen palette and pendant chrome
test/grbl.test.js  node --test: streamer flow control + status parsing
reference/         HAAS operator manuals (PDF) for layout fidelity
```

One file per HAAS display page, because each page is a distinct concept a student
will look up. Everything else stays collapsed until it earns a split.

### Transport interface

Three implementations behind four methods, so nothing above knows which is in use:

```js
{ connect(), send(str), sendRealtime(byte), onLine(cb), disconnect() }
```

- **WebSocket** — connect **without** the `webui-v3` subprotocol. Confirmed in
  `src/webui/server.c:180-193`: that subprotocol switches the socket to binary
  frames and hands text frames to the WebUI's own JSON handler. Omitting it gives
  a plain bidirectional grbl stream — telnet semantics over a websocket, which is
  exactly what a sender wants.
- **Web Serial** — `navigator.serial.requestPort()`, 115200 8N1, `TextDecoderStream`
  split on `\n`. Needs a **secure context**: works on `localhost` and HTTPS,
  silently unavailable on a plain-HTTP LAN address. Chrome/Edge only.
- **Simulator** — same interface, no I/O.

Because the built app is served from the board itself, the CORS question that
would dog a separately-hosted sender does not arise. It stays hostable from a dev
server too, since the websocket path is CORS-exempt.

### Job streaming

The one piece of genuinely non-trivial logic. Character-counting flow control:

- Keep a queue of the byte lengths of lines sent but not acknowledged.
- Send the next line only while `sum(pending) + len(next) < rxBuffer`.
- On each `ok` or `error:N`, pop the oldest length.
- `error:N` mid-job halts the stream and raises an alarm on the ALARMS page.

`rxBuffer` is a **calibration knob, seeded from the board**: default 128 (safe for
any classic GRBL), then raised to the value the board reports in `Bf:` — 1023 on
this ClearCore. Never trust a hardcoded constant here.

Status polling: send `?` at ~5 Hz from the sender, identically on all three
transports. This sidesteps the `$397` WebUI-push mechanism the ClearCore README
documents, which only works for websocket clients that identify as WebUI.

This gets the project's one required test (`test/grbl.test.js`, `node --test`):
feed a scripted line list plus acks and assert in-flight bytes never exceed the
buffer and every line is sent exactly once.

### Simulator

A virtual grblHAL speaking the same wire protocol: `ok` per accepted line,
`<Idle|MPos:...|FS:...|Bf:...>` on `?`, honours `!` / `~` / `0x18` and the
override bytes, walks position along each move at the programmed feedrate, and
can be told to throw a limit alarm so students see the ALARMS page do something.

Deliberately no acceleration planner and no lookahead — position is linearly
interpolated per move, indistinguishable from the real thing for teaching the
operator workflow. Marked with a `ponytail:` comment naming that ceiling.

---

## HAAS → grblHAL mapping

The substance of the project; this table belongs in the repo README too. Real-time
byte values verified against the Grbl v1.1 interface documentation.

| HAAS pendant control | grbl / grblHAL |
|---|---|
| CYCLE START | `~` (0x7E), or start the streamer |
| FEED HOLD | `!` (0x21) |
| RESET | soft reset 0x18 |
| EMERGENCY STOP | 0x18 + stop streaming (real E-stop is hardware — say so in HELP) |
| FEEDRATE 100% / +10% / −10% | 0x90 / 0x91 / 0x92 |
| SPINDLE 100% / +10% / −10% | 0x99 / 0x9A / 0x9B |
| RAPID 100% / 50% / 25% | 0x95 / 0x96 / 0x97 |
| RAPID 5% | **no grbl equivalent** — see gaps |
| COOLNT | flood toggle 0xA0 |
| SPINDLE CW / CCW / STOP | `M3` / `M4` / `M5` (0x9E only acts in HOLD) |
| HANDLE JOG + increment | `$J=G91 F<rate> X<inc>`; jog cancel 0x85 |
| ZERO RET → ALL | `$H` homing cycle |
| ZERO RET → HOME G28 | `G28` |
| POSITION: MACHINE | `MPos:` from the status report |
| POSITION: WORK G54 | `MPos − WCO` (`WCO:` arrives every 10–30 reports) |
| POSITION: DIST TO GO | computed sender-side from the running block's target |
| POSITION: OPERATOR | sender-side zeroable display, no grbl equivalent |
| OFFSET → WORK G54–G59 | `G10 L2 P1..6`, read back with `$#` |
| OFFSET → TOOL length | sender-owned tool table, emitted as `G43.1 Z−<offset>` |
| ALARMS | `ALARM:N` / `error:N`, shown with both the grbl code and HAAS-style text |
| CURRENT COMMANDS | modal state from `$G`, live feed/speed from `FS:` |
| MDI | typed block sent directly |
| LIST PROG | programs stored by O-number in browser storage |

### Gaps to design around, not paper over

- **RAPID 5%** does not exist in grbl (only 100/50/25). Render the key, and have it
  post a "not supported on this control" message rather than silently lying.
- **Tool table**: this build has `N_TOOLS 0`, and base GRBL only has dynamic TLO.
  So aaSender owns the authoritative tool table and emits `G43.1 Z−<offset>` when a
  program calls `G43 H<n>`. Works on every board and keeps the OFFSET page honest.
- **G154 P1–P99** extended work offsets have no grbl equivalent. Ship G54–G59;
  G154 later if wanted.
- **`Ln:` line number** is a compile-time option and normally off — track the
  running line sender-side from the streamer.
- **Units**: HAAS shops usually run inch, grbl defaults to mm. Read `$13` and show
  the active unit on screen rather than assuming.

---

## Build phases

Each phase ends somewhere demonstrable.

1. **Pipeline.** `transport.js` + `sim.js` + `grbl.js` + the streamer test + a
   throwaway debug screen. Ends with: a g-code file streams to the simulator and
   position advances. No HAAS look yet.
2. **Pendant chrome.** `Pendant.jsx`, `haas.css`, `keys.js`, POSITION page, jog.
   Keypad is transcribed from `images/haas2.jpg` and the operator manual. Ends
   with: the pendant looks right and HANDLE JOG moves the simulated machine.
3. **Run a part.** LIST PROG, MEM mode, CYCLE START / FEED HOLD / RESET, PROGRAM
   page with the running block highlighted, the OVERRIDES key block. Ends with:
   a student loads a program and runs it exactly as on a HAAS.
4. **Offsets and status.** OFFSET (tool + work), CURRENT COMMANDS, ALARMS with the
   grbl→HAAS code mapping, PART ZERO SET / TOOL OFSET MESUR entry workflow.
5. **Programming.** EDIT mode with HAAS word-level INSERT / ALTER / DELETE / UNDO,
   and MDI. This is the fiddliest HAAS behaviour — the cursor selects a *word*
   (address + value), not a character — so it gets its own phase.
6. **Hardware bring-up.** WebSocket against the ClearCore at its DHCP address,
   Web Serial over USB CDC, then install to SD `/www` and run from the board.

---

## Verification

- **Streamer logic**: `node --test test/grbl.test.js` — the only unit test, covering
  flow control and status parsing.
- **Whole app, no hardware**: `npm run dev`, drive the simulator in Chrome. Every
  page, mode and key is exercisable this way; this is also the classroom mode, so
  it has to work.
- **Against the real board**: connect by WebSocket to the ClearCore's address and
  by Web Serial to `2890:8022`. Confirm `?` polling drives the DRO, `$#` populates
  the OFFSET page, a jog produces motion, and a job streams without a buffer
  overrun (watch `Bf:`).
- **Installed on the board**: build, gzip, `GET /sdfiles?action=createdir&filename=www&path=/`,
  multipart-POST to `/sdfiles`, load `http://<board-ip>/`.
  **Back up the existing `/www/index.html.gz` first** — installing aaSender
  replaces the working ESP3D-WebUI, and that UI is the fallback if aaSender
  misbehaves on the bench.

# aaSender — a HAAS-lookalike g-code sender for grblHAL

## Context

`/home/holla/aaSender` is empty apart from `images/haas1.jpg` and `images/haas2.jpg`,
two photos of a classic (pre-NGC, green-screen) HAAS mill pendant. The goal is a
browser-based g-code sender whose entire operator interface is a replica of that
pendant, so students learning on HAAS machines can practice the real workflow —
modes, DISPLAY pages, HANDLE JOG, CYCLE START, offsets, on-control editing —
against a hobby-class grblHAL machine, a USB GRBL board, or nothing at all.

The reference for "the communication and operation works" is
[ESP3D-WEBUI](https://github.com/luc-github/ESP3D-WEBUI/tree/3.0/dist/CNC/GRBLHal).
We are not forking its UI (that is a conventional sender layout); we reuse its
proven approach to transport and job streaming and replace everything above that
with the HAAS pendant.

**Decisions already made with the user:**
- Three transports: grblHAL over network (ESP3D-style), Web Serial over USB, and a
  built-in simulator so a classroom seat needs no hardware.
- Full pendant replica — clickable keypad and green screen, operated the way a real
  HAAS is.
- Classic green-screen generation (the one in `images/`), not NGC.
- Scope: operator essentials **plus** programming — EDIT mode, MDI, and offset entry.

---

## Architecture

Vite + Preact, static build, no backend. Preact because ESP3D-WEBUI uses it (any
reference code transfers) and because a pendant with ~10 display pages, a program
editor and live status needs real state management. Everything else is stdlib or
plain DOM.

```
index.html
vite.config.js
src/
  main.jsx
  grbl.js          status/ok/error/alarm parsing, error+alarm code tables,
                   character-counting job streamer
  transport.js     one interface, three impls: WebSocket | Web Serial | Simulator
  sim.js           virtual grblHAL machine (no hardware needed)
  haas.js          HAAS machine model: modes, work/tool offsets, timers,
                   grbl->HAAS alarm mapping
  keys.js          pendant key table + key -> action dispatch
  ui/Pendant.jsx   bezel, logo, E-stop, handle-jog dial, keypad
  ui/Screen.jsx    green screen frame + DISPLAY page router
  ui/pages/*.jsx   Position, Program, Offset, CurrCmds, Alarms, Setng, ListProg, Help
  haas.css         the green-screen palette and pendant chrome
test/grbl.test.js  node --test: streamer flow control + status parsing
```

One file per HAAS display page because each page is a distinct concept a student
will look up; everything else stays collapsed until it earns a split.

### Transport interface

All three transports expose the same four things, so nothing above this layer
knows which is in use:

```js
{ connect(), send(str), sendRealtime(byte), onLine(cb), disconnect() }
```

- **WebSocket** — the ESP3D/grblHAL network path. Board pushes status and terminal
  output; we push commands. Real-time bytes go over the same socket.
- **Web Serial** — `navigator.serial.requestPort()`, 115200 8N1, a
  `TextDecoderStream` split on `\n`. Requires a **secure context**: works on
  `localhost` and any HTTPS origin, silently absent on plain-HTTP LAN addresses.
  Chrome/Edge only — Firefox and Safari do not implement Web Serial.
- **Simulator** — same interface, no I/O. See below.

**Known risk to settle in Phase 1:** when the app is *not* served from the board,
browser CORS may block plain HTTP calls to grblHAL's `/command` endpoint.
WebSockets are exempt from CORS, so the mitigation is to drive everything over the
websocket and use HTTP only for file upload. Fallback if that proves impossible:
build to a gzipped bundle and serve it from the board's flash exactly as
ESP3D-WEBUI does.

### Job streaming

The one piece of genuinely non-trivial logic. Character-counting flow control,
the same algorithm every working GRBL sender uses:

- Keep a queue of the byte lengths of lines sent but not yet acknowledged.
- Send the next line only while `sum(pending) + len(next) < RX_BUFFER_SIZE`.
- On each `ok` or `error:N`, pop the oldest length.
- `error:N` during a job halts the stream and raises an alarm on the ALARMS page.

Buffer size is a **calibration knob**, not a constant: 128 bytes is the safe
classic-GRBL value, grblHAL boards are typically larger and report free space in
the `Bf:` status field. Default 128, settable, and cross-checked against `Bf:` at
runtime.

This gets the project's one required test (`test/grbl.test.js`, `node --test`):
feed a scripted line list plus acks and assert the in-flight byte count never
exceeds the buffer and every line goes out exactly once.

### Simulator

A virtual grblHAL that responds to the same wire protocol: `ok` per accepted line,
`<Idle|MPos:...|FS:...>` on `?`, honours `!`/`~`/`0x18` and the override bytes,
walks the position along each move at the programmed feedrate, and can be told to
throw a limit-switch alarm so students see the ALARMS page do something.

Deliberately no acceleration planner and no lookahead — position is linearly
interpolated per move, which is indistinguishable from the real thing for teaching
the operator workflow. Marked with a `ponytail:` comment naming that ceiling.

---

## HAAS → grblHAL mapping

This table is the substance of the project and belongs in the repo README too.
All real-time byte values verified against the Grbl v1.1 interface docs.

| HAAS pendant control | grbl / grblHAL |
|---|---|
| CYCLE START | `~` (0x7E), or start the streamer |
| FEED HOLD | `!` (0x21) |
| RESET | soft reset 0x18 |
| EMERGENCY STOP | 0x18 + stop streaming (real E-stop is hardware; note this in HELP) |
| FEEDRATE 100% / +10% / −10% | 0x90 / 0x91 / 0x92 |
| SPINDLE 100% / +10% / −10% | 0x99 / 0x9A / 0x9B |
| RAPID 100% / 50% / 25% | 0x95 / 0x96 / 0x97 |
| RAPID 5% | **no grbl equivalent** — see gaps below |
| COOLNT | flood toggle 0xA0 |
| SPINDLE CW / CCW / STOP | `M3` / `M4` / `M5` (0x9E only works in HOLD) |
| HANDLE JOG + increment | `$J=G91 F<rate> X<inc>`; jog cancel 0x85 on dial stop |
| ZERO RET → ALL | `$H` homing cycle |
| ZERO RET → HOME G28 | `G28` |
| POSITION: MACHINE | `MPos:` from the status report |
| POSITION: WORK G54 | `MPos − WCO` (grbl reports `WCO:` every 10–30 reports) |
| POSITION: DIST TO GO | computed sender-side from the running block's target |
| POSITION: OPERATOR | sender-side zeroable display, no grbl equivalent |
| OFFSET → WORK G54–G59 | `G10 L2 P1..6`, read back via `$#` |
| OFFSET → TOOL length | sender-owned tool table, emitted as `G43.1 Z−<offset>` |
| ALARMS page | `ALARM:N` and `error:N` codes, shown with both numbers and HAAS-style text |
| CURRENT COMMANDS | modal state from `$G`, live feed/speed from `FS:` |
| MDI | line typed on the pendant, sent directly |
| LIST PROG | programs stored by O-number in browser storage |

### Known gaps to design around, not paper over

- **RAPID 5%** does not exist in grbl (only 100/50/25). Show the key, and have it
  display a "not supported on this control" message rather than lying.
- **Tool table**: base GRBL has only dynamic TLO (`G43.1`); grblHAL has a real tool
  table but only in some builds. So the *sender* owns the authoritative tool table
  and emits `G43.1 Z−<offset>` when the program calls `G43 H<n>`. This works on
  every board and keeps the HAAS offsets page honest.
- **G154 P1–P99** extended work offsets have no grbl equivalent. Ship G54–G59 in
  the OFFSET page; G154 is a later addition if the user wants it.
- **`Ln:` line number** in status reports is a compile-time option and usually off.
  Track the running line sender-side from the streamer instead.

---

*(HAAS screen-layout and ESP3D transport research still landing — pages, keypad
groups and phasing to be filled in)*

# aaSender — a HAAS-lookalike g-code sender for grblHAL / ClearCore

## Context

`/home/holla/aaSender` is empty apart from `images/haas1.jpg` and `images/haas2.jpg`,
photos of a classic (pre-NGC, green-screen) HAAS mill pendant. The goal is a
browser-based g-code sender whose entire operator interface replicates that
pendant, so students learning on HAAS machines can practice the real workflow —
modes, DISPLAY pages, HANDLE JOG, CYCLE START, offsets, on-control editing —
against a hobby-class grblHAL machine or nothing at all.

The target hardware is the companion project **`/home/holla/grblhal-clearcore`**
(Teknic ClearCore, SAME53, bare-metal grblHAL, 4-axis XYZA), already bench-verified
with Ethernet, telnet, WebSocket, HTTP, the WebUI plugin, SD job streaming and USB
CDC. It currently serves ESP3D-WebUI v3 from SD `/www`. aaSender is the
HAAS-skinned replacement for that UI.

**Decisions already made with the user:**
- Three transports: network WebSocket, Web Serial over USB, and a built-in
  simulator so a classroom seat needs no hardware.
- Full pendant replica — clickable keypad and green screen, operated like a real HAAS.
- Classic green-screen generation (the one in `images/`), not NGC.
- Scope: operator essentials **plus** programming — EDIT mode, MDI, offset entry.

---

## Verified against the live board

The ClearCore was powered up at `192.168.0.113` during planning, so the transport
design below is **measured, not assumed**. Open ports: 23 (telnet), 80 (HTTP),
81 (WebSocket).

Identity from `$I`:

```
[VER:1.1f.20260726:]  [OPT:VNML,100,1024,4,0]  [AXS:4:XYZA]
[NEWOPT:ENUMS,RT+,TC,SED,ETH,FS,SD]  [FIRMWARE:grblHAL]
```

A live status report:

```
<Idle|MPos:111.470,-192.628,5.000,0.000|Bf:100,1023|Ln:187756|FS:0,0|Ov:100,100,100>
```

**The load-bearing finding:** the WebSocket carries the grbl stream **only when the
client negotiates the `webui-v3` subprotocol.** Connecting with no subprotocol, or
with `arduino`, completes the handshake and then passes nothing in either
direction — verified with both text and binary frames. With `webui-v3` the socket
is fully bidirectional: `$I` sent over it returned its reply over it.

Other measured facts and what each one changes:

| Measured | Consequence |
|---|---|
| `webui-v3` required for any data flow | The network transport must request that subprotocol. Not optional. |
| On connect, two text frames arrive: `currentID:<n>`, `activeID:<n>` | ESP3D session handshake — filter these before the grbl parser sees them. |
| Status reports auto-push every 250 ms (`$397=250` already set) | Do not blindly poll `?`. Poll only if no report arrives for ~500 ms, which self-tunes across all three transports. |
| `Ln:187756` present in status | **Running line number comes free** — no need to track it sender-side, contrary to the usual grbl assumption. |
| `[OPT:...,100,1024,...]` and `Bf:100,1023` | Planner 100 blocks, RX buffer **1024** bytes, not the classic 128. Read it at connect. |
| `[AXS:4:XYZA]` | Position and offset pages are 4-axis. |
| `[NEWOPT:...,TC,...]` | Firmware advertises tool-change support. |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every HTTP response | No CORS problem even from a laptop dev server — the earlier worry is dead. |
| `GET /command?cmd=…` returns only `ok`; output goes to the socket | HTTP is a command sink, the socket is the data source. Since the socket also accepts writes, **we can ignore HTTP entirely for commands.** |
| `GET /` serves 93,373 bytes gzipped from SD `/www` | aaSender installs the same way, and must fit a comparable budget. |
| `N_TOOLS 0` in `src/grbl/config.h` | Board has **no tool table** — the sender must own it. |
| Repo is MIT; grblHAL core is GPLv3 | aaSender links no grblHAL code, so MIT is fine. |

Worth reporting back to the companion project: a conventional sender (ioSender,
gSender) connecting over WebSocket without `webui-v3` will see a dead socket. That
looks like a firmware-side gap rather than intended behaviour, but it is out of
scope here — aaSender simply negotiates `webui-v3`.

---

## Architecture

Vite + Preact, static build, no backend. Preact because ESP3D-WEBUI uses it (any
reference transfers), it is ~3 KB, and a pendant with ten display pages, a program
editor and live status needs real state management. Everything else is stdlib or
plain DOM.

The build must produce **one self-contained gzipped file** to sit on the board's SD
card. `vite-plugin-singlefile` inlines JS/CSS into `index.html`; a build step gzips
it. ESP3D-WebUI is 91 KB gzipped, so the budget is **≤150 KB gzipped**, enforced by
a build-script check that fails loudly when exceeded.

```
index.html
vite.config.js
src/
  main.jsx
  grbl.js          status/ok/error/alarm parsing, error+alarm tables,
                   character-counting job streamer
  transport.js     one interface, three impls: WebSocket | Web Serial | Simulator
  sim.js           virtual grblHAL machine (no hardware needed)
  haas.js          HAAS machine model: modes, work/tool offsets, timers,
                   grbl -> HAAS alarm mapping
  keys.js          pendant key table + key -> action dispatch
  ui/Pendant.jsx   bezel, logo, E-stop, handle-jog dial, keypad
  ui/Screen.jsx    green screen frame + DISPLAY page router
  ui/pages/*.jsx   Position, Program, Offset, CurrCmds, Alarms, Setng, ListProg, Help
  haas.css         green-screen palette and pendant chrome
test/grbl.test.js  node --test: streamer flow control + status parsing
reference/         HAAS operator manuals (PDF) for layout fidelity
```

One file per HAAS display page, because each is a distinct concept a student will
look up. Everything else stays collapsed until it earns a split.

### Transport interface

Three implementations behind four methods, so nothing above knows which is in use:

```js
{ connect(), send(str), sendRealtime(byte), onLine(cb), disconnect() }
```

- **WebSocket** — `new WebSocket("ws://<ip>:81/", ["webui-v3"])`, `binaryType =
  "arraybuffer"`, decode frames with `TextDecoder`, drop the `currentID:` /
  `activeID:` handshake lines, split the rest on `\n`. Writes go over the same
  socket. No HTTP needed except for installing the app itself.
- **Web Serial** — `navigator.serial.requestPort()`, 115200 8N1,

`/home/holla/aaSender` is empty apart from `images/haas1.jpg` and `images/haas2.jpg`,

pendant, so students learning on HAAS machines can practice the real workflow —

The target hardware is the companion project **`/home/holla/grblhal-clearcore`**
(Teknic ClearCore, SAME53, bare-metal grblHAL, 4-axis XYZA), already bench-verified
with Ethernet, telnet, WebSocket, HTTP, the WebUI plugin, SD job streaming and USB
CDC. It currently serves ESP3D-WebUI v3 from SD `/www`. aaSender is the
HAAS-skinned replacement for that UI.

**Decisions already made with the user:**
- Three transports: network WebSocket, Web Serial over USB, and a built-in
  simulator so a classroom seat needs no hardware.
- Full pendant replica — clickable keypad and green screen, operated like a real HAAS.
- Classic green-screen generation (the one in `images/`), not NGC.
- Scope: operator essentials **plus** programming — EDIT mode, MDI, offset entry.

---

The ClearCore was powered up at `192.168.0.113` during planning, so the transport
design below is **measured, not assumed**. Open ports: 23 (telnet), 80 (HTTP),
81 (WebSocket).

Identity from `$I`:

```
[VER:1.1f.20260726:]  [OPT:VNML,100,1024,4,0]  [AXS:4:XYZA]
[NEWOPT:ENUMS,RT+,TC,SED,ETH,FS,SD]  [FIRMWARE:grblHAL]
```

A live status report:

```
<Idle|MPos:111.470,-192.628,5.000,0.000|Bf:100,1023|Ln:187756|FS:0,0|Ov:100,100,100>
```

**The load-bearing finding:** the WebSocket carries the grbl stream **only when the
client negotiates the `webui-v3` subprotocol.** Connecting with no subprotocol, or
with `arduino`, completes the handshake and then passes nothing in either
direction — verified with both text and binary frames. With `webui-v3` the socket
is fully bidirectional: `$I` sent over it returned its reply over it.

# aaSender — a HAAS-lookalike g-code sender for grblHAL / ClearCore

## Context

`/home/holla/aaSender` is empty apart from `images/haas1.jpg` and `images/haas2.jpg`,
photos of a classic (pre-NGC, green-screen) HAAS mill pendant. The goal is a
browser-based g-code sender whose entire operator interface replicates that
pendant, so students learning on HAAS machines can practice the real workflow —
modes, DISPLAY pages, HANDLE JOG, CYCLE START, offsets, on-control editing —
against a hobby-class grblHAL machine or nothing at all.

The target hardware is the companion project **`/home/holla/grblhal-clearcore`**
(Teknic ClearCore, SAME53, bare-metal grblHAL, 4-axis XYZA), already bench-verified
with Ethernet, telnet, WebSocket, HTTP, the WebUI plugin, SD job streaming and USB
CDC. It currently serves ESP3D-WebUI v3 from SD `/www`. aaSender is the
HAAS-skinned replacement for that UI.

**Decisions already made with the user:**
- Three transports: network WebSocket, Web Serial over USB, and a built-in
  simulator so a classroom seat needs no hardware.
- Full pendant replica — clickable keypad and green screen, operated like a real HAAS.
- Classic green-screen generation (the one in `images/`), not NGC.
- Scope: operator essentials **plus** programming — EDIT mode, MDI, offset entry.

---

## Verified against the live board

The ClearCore was powered up at `192.168.0.113` during planning, so the transport
design below is **measured, not assumed**. Open ports: 23 (telnet), 80 (HTTP),
81 (WebSocket).

Identity from `$I`:

```
[VER:1.1f.20260726:]  [OPT:VNML,100,1024,4,0]  [AXS:4:XYZA]
[NEWOPT:ENUMS,RT+,TC,SED,ETH,FS,SD]  [FIRMWARE:grblHAL]
```

A live status report:

```
<Idle|MPos:111.470,-192.628,5.000,0.000|Bf:100,1023|Ln:187756|FS:0,0|Ov:100,100,100>
```

**The load-bearing finding:** the WebSocket carries the grbl stream **only when the
client negotiates the `webui-v3` subprotocol.** Connecting with no subprotocol, or
with `arduino`, completes the handshake and then passes nothing in either
direction — verified with both text and binary frames. With `webui-v3` the socket
is fully bidirectional: `$I` sent over it returned its reply over it.

Other measured facts and what each one changes:

| Measured | Consequence |
|---|---|
| `webui-v3` required for any data flow | The network transport must request that subprotocol. Not optional. |
| On connect, two text frames arrive: `currentID:<n>`, `activeID:<n>` | ESP3D session handshake — filter these before the grbl parser sees them. |
| Status reports auto-push every 250 ms (`$397=250` already set) | Do not blindly poll `?`. Poll only if no report arrives for ~500 ms, which self-tunes across all three transports. |
| `Ln:187756` present in status | **Running line number comes free** — no need to track it sender-side, contrary to the usual grbl assumption. |
| `[OPT:...,100,1024,...]` and `Bf:100,1023` | Planner 100 blocks, RX buffer **1024** bytes, not the classic 128. Read it at connect. |
| `[AXS:4:XYZA]` | Position and offset pages are 4-axis. |
| `[NEWOPT:...,TC,...]` | Firmware advertises tool-change support. |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every HTTP response | No CORS problem even from a laptop dev server — the earlier worry is dead. |
| `GET /command?cmd=…` returns only `ok`; output goes to the socket | HTTP is a command sink, the socket is the data source. Since the socket also accepts writes, **we can ignore HTTP entirely for commands.** |
| `GET /` serves 93,373 bytes gzipped from SD `/www` | aaSender installs the same way, and must fit a comparable budget. |
| `N_TOOLS 0` in `src/grbl/config.h` | Board has **no tool table** — the sender must own it. |
| Repo is MIT; grblHAL core is GPLv3 | aaSender links no grblHAL code, so MIT is fine. |

Worth reporting back to the companion project: a conventional sender (ioSender,
gSender) connecting over WebSocket without `webui-v3` will see a dead socket. That
looks like a firmware-side gap rather than intended behaviour, but it is out of
scope here — aaSender simply negotiates `webui-v3`.

---

## Architecture

Vite + Preact, static build, no backend. Preact because ESP3D-WEBUI uses it (any
reference transfers), it is ~3 KB, and a pendant with ten display pages, a program
editor and live status needs real state management. Everything else is stdlib or
plain DOM.

The build must produce **one self-contained gzipped file** to sit on the board's SD
card. `vite-plugin-singlefile` inlines JS/CSS into `index.html`; a build step gzips
it. ESP3D-WebUI is 91 KB gzipped, so the budget is **≤150 KB gzipped**, enforced by
a build-script check that fails loudly when exceeded.

```
index.html
vite.config.js
src/
  main.jsx
  grbl.js          status/ok/error/alarm parsing, error+alarm tables,
                   character-counting job streamer
  transport.js     one interface, three impls: WebSocket | Web Serial | Simulator
  sim.js           virtual grblHAL machine (no hardware needed)
  haas.js          HAAS machine model: modes, work/tool offsets, timers,
                   grbl -> HAAS alarm mapping
  keys.js          pendant key table + key -> action dispatch
  ui/Pendant.jsx   bezel, logo, E-stop, handle-jog dial, keypad
  ui/Screen.jsx    green screen frame + DISPLAY page router
  ui/pages/*.jsx   Position, Program, Offset, CurrCmds, Alarms, Setng, ListProg, Help
  haas.css         green-screen palette and pendant chrome
test/grbl.test.js  node --test: streamer flow control + status parsing
reference/         HAAS operator manuals (PDF) for layout fidelity — still empty
```

**On reference material:** an automated attempt to fetch a classic HAAS mill
operator's manual came back empty-handed; HAAS keeps current manuals behind its own
portal. This does not block Phase 2 — `images/haas2.jpg` is legible enough to read
every key legend (DISPLAY / MODE / CURSOR / OVERRIDES groups, the jog block, the
alpha-numeric pad), and that photo is the primary source for the keypad. A manual
would mainly improve the *screen page* layouts in Phases 3–5, so it is worth the
user dropping a PDF into `reference/` before those phases if they have one.

One file per HAAS display page, because each is a distinct concept a student will
look up. Everything else stays collapsed until it earns a split.

### Transport interface

Three implementations behind four methods, so nothing above knows which is in use:

```js
{ connect(), send(str), sendRealtime(byte), onLine(cb), disconnect() }
```

- **WebSocket** — `new WebSocket("ws://<ip>:81/", ["webui-v3"])`, `binaryType =
  "arraybuffer"`, decode frames with `TextDecoder`, drop the `currentID:` /
  `activeID:` handshake lines, split the rest on `\n`. Writes go over the same
  socket. No HTTP needed except for installing the app itself.
- **Web Serial** — `navigator.serial.requestPort()`, 115200 8N1,
  `TextDecoderStream` split on `\n`. Needs a **secure context**: works on
  `localhost` and HTTPS, unavailable on a plain-HTTP LAN address. Chrome/Edge only.
  The board enumerates as `2890:8022`.
- **Simulator** — same interface, no I/O.

Status acquisition is uniform: if no `<...>` report has arrived for 500 ms, send
`?`. On the ClearCore's auto-push that timer never fires; on serial it becomes a
5 Hz poll. One rule, three transports, no per-transport special-casing.

### Job streaming

The one piece of genuinely non-trivial logic. Character-counting flow control:

- Keep a queue of the byte lengths of lines sent but not acknowledged.
- Send the next line only while `sum(pending) + len(next) < rxBuffer`.
- On each `ok` or `error:N`, pop the oldest length.
- `error:N` mid-job halts the stream and raises an alarm on the ALARMS page.

`rxBuffer` is a **calibration knob seeded from the board**: default 128 (safe for
any classic GRBL), raised to the value parsed from `[OPT:...]` / `Bf:` at connect —
1024 on this ClearCore. Never a hardcoded constant.

This gets the project's one required test (`test/grbl.test.js`, `node --test`):
feed a scripted line list plus acks and assert in-flight bytes never exceed the
buffer and every line is sent exactly once.

### Simulator

A virtual grblHAL speaking the same wire protocol: `ok` per accepted line,
`<Idle|MPos:...|Bf:...|Ln:...|FS:...>` on `?` and on a 250 ms auto-push, honours
`!` / `~` / `0x18` and the override bytes, walks position along each move at the
programmed feedrate, and can be told to throw a limit alarm so students see the
ALARMS page do something.

Deliberately no acceleration planner and no lookahead — position is linearly
interpolated per move, indistinguishable from the real thing for teaching the
operator workflow. Marked with a `ponytail:` comment naming that ceiling.

---

## HAAS → grblHAL mapping

The substance of the project; this table belongs in the repo README too. Real-time
byte values are from the Grbl v1.1 interface documentation.

| HAAS pendant control | grbl / grblHAL |
|---|---|
| CYCLE START | `~` (0x7E), or start the streamer |
| FEED HOLD | `!` (0x21) |
| RESET | soft reset 0x18 |
| EMERGENCY STOP | 0x18 + stop streaming (real E-stop is hardware — say so in HELP) |
| FEEDRATE 100% / +10% / −10% | 0x90 / 0x91 / 0x92 |
| SPINDLE 100% / +10% / −10% | 0x99 / 0x9A / 0x9B |
| RAPID 100% / 50% / 25% | 0x95 / 0x96 / 0x97 |
| RAPID 5% | **no grbl equivalent** — see gaps |
| COOLNT | flood toggle 0xA0 |
| SPINDLE CW / CCW / STOP | `M3` / `M4` / `M5` (0x9E only acts in HOLD) |
| HANDLE JOG + increment | `$J=G91 F<rate> X<inc>`; jog cancel 0x85 |
| ZERO RET → ALL | `$H` homing cycle |
| ZERO RET → HOME G28 | `G28` |
| POSITION: MACHINE | `MPos:` from the status report |
| POSITION: WORK G54 | `MPos − WCO` (`WCO:` arrives every 10–30 reports) |
| POSITION: DIST TO GO | computed from the running block's target |
| POSITION: OPERATOR | sender-side zeroable display, no grbl equivalent |
| Running block highlight | `Ln:` from the status report — confirmed present |
| OFFSET → WORK G54–G59 | `G10 L2 P1..6`, read back with `$#` |
| OFFSET → WORK G154 P1–P3 | `G59.1` / `G59.2` / `G59.3` — the board reports all nine |
| OFFSET → TOOL length | sender-owned tool table, emitted as `G43.1 Z−<offset>` |
| ALARMS | `ALARM:N` / `error:N`, shown with both the grbl code and HAAS-style text |
| CURRENT COMMANDS | modal string from `$G`, live feed/speed from `FS:` |
| MDI | typed block sent directly |
| LIST PROG | programs stored by O-number in browser storage |

### Gaps to design around, not paper over

- **RAPID 5%** does not exist in grbl (only 100/50/25). Render the key, and have it
  post a "not supported on this control" message rather than silently lying.
- **Tool table**: this build has `N_TOOLS 0`, and base GRBL has only dynamic TLO.
  aaSender owns the authoritative tool table and emits `G43.1 Z−<offset>` when a
  program calls `G43 H<n>`. Works on every board and keeps the OFFSET page honest.
- **G154 P1–P99**: the board reports nine coordinate systems, so `G59.1`–`G59.3`
  can back HAAS `G154 P1`–`P3`. P4 upward has no equivalent; the OFFSET page shows
  the three that exist rather than pretending to ninety-nine.
- **Units**: the board reports `$13=0`, i.e. **millimetres**, while HAAS shops
  usually run inch. The pendant must offer G20/G21 and display the active unit —
  the one place where a faithful HAAS replica would mislead a student about the
  machine underneath it.

Measured reference output the pages are built against:

```
$#  → [G54:0,0,0,0] … [G59.3:0,0,0,0] [G28:…] [G30:…] [G92:…]
      [TLO:0.000,0.000,0.000,0.000]  (per-axis, not a scalar)
      [PRB:0.000,0.000,0.000,0.000:0]
$G  → [GC:G1 G54 G17 G21 G90 G94 G49 G98 G50 M5 M9 T0 F2540 S0.]
```

`$#` feeds the OFFSET page, `$G` feeds CURRENT COMMANDS more or less verbatim.

---

## Build phases

Each phase ends somewhere demonstrable.

1. **Pipeline.** `transport.js` + `sim.js` + `grbl.js` + the streamer test + a
   throwaway debug screen. Ends with: a g-code file streams to the simulator and
   position advances.
2. **Pendant chrome.** `Pendant.jsx`, `haas.css`, `keys.js`, POSITION page, jog.
   The keypad is transcribed from `images/haas2.jpg`, which is legible enough to
   read every key legend, cross-checked against an operator manual in `reference/`.
   Ends with: the pendant looks right and HANDLE JOG moves the simulated machine.
3. **Run a part.** LIST PROG, MEM mode, CYCLE START / FEED HOLD / RESET, PROGRAM
   page with the running block highlighted (driven by `Ln:`), the OVERRIDES block.
   Ends with: a student loads a program and runs it as on a HAAS.
4. **Offsets and status.** OFFSET (tool + work), CURRENT COMMANDS, ALARMS with the
   grbl→HAAS code mapping, PART ZERO SET / TOOL OFSET MESUR entry workflow.
5. **Programming.** EDIT mode with HAAS word-level INSERT / ALTER / DELETE / UNDO,
   and MDI. The cursor selects a *word* (address + value), not a character, which
   is why this gets its own phase.
6. **Hardware bring-up.** WebSocket to the ClearCore, Web Serial over USB CDC, then
   install to SD `/www` and run from the board.

---

## Verification

- **Streamer logic**: `node --test test/grbl.test.js` — the only unit test, covering
  flow control and status parsing.
- **Whole app, no hardware**: `npm run dev`, drive the simulator in Chrome. Every
  page, mode and key is exercisable this way; this is also the classroom mode, so
  it has to work.
- **Against the real board** (live at `192.168.0.113` during planning): connect by
  WebSocket with `webui-v3` and by Web Serial to `2890:8022`. Confirm the DRO
  tracks, `$#` populates the OFFSET page, a jog produces motion, and a job streams
  without a buffer overrun (watch `Bf:`).
- **Installed on the board**: build, gzip,
  `GET /sdfiles?action=createdir&filename=www&path=/`, multipart-POST to `/sdfiles`,
  load `http://<board-ip>/`.
  **Back up the existing `/www/index.html.gz` first** — installing aaSender replaces
  the working ESP3D-WebUI, which is the fallback if aaSender misbehaves on the bench.

### Safety note for bench testing

The board reports `MPos:111.470,-192.628,5.000,0.000`, so it is a real configured
machine, not a bare desk board. Every hardware phase should start with the machine
clear of stock and the spindle off; jog and homing tests come before any job
streaming test.

Stopping there — I won't push the plan for approval again until you say so.

Where things stand: the plan is written to `/home/holla/.claude/plans/this-is-a-research-partitioned-seal.md`. The most valuable part of this session turned out not to be the web research but the fact that your ClearCore was powered up at `192.168.0.113`, so I could test the transport assumptions directly instead of guessing.

**The finding that matters most:** the WebSocket on port 81 only carries the grbl stream if the client negotiates the `webui-v3` subprotocol. Connecting with no subprotocol, or with `arduino`, completes the handshake cleanly and then passes nothing in either direction — I tried both text and binary frames. With `webui-v3` it's fully bidirectional: I sent `$I` over the socket and got the reply back on it. That's worth knowing for your firmware project too, because it means ioSender or gSender connecting over WebSocket would see a dead socket and no obvious reason why.

Three of my initial assumptions were wrong and are now corrected in the plan: the RX buffer is 1024 bytes rather than the classic 128; `Ln:` *is* present in status reports, so the running-block highlight comes free instead of needing sender-side tracking; and the board reports nine work coordinate systems (`G54`–`G59` plus `G59.1`–`G59.3`), so HAAS `G154 P1`–`P3` has a real backing store. Also, every HTTP response carries `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, which kills the CORS concern I'd built a mitigation around.

And the two background research agents on ESP3D and the HAAS UI never reported back; the ESP3D one is moot now that I read your firmware source directly, but the HAAS UI one would have refined the display-page details.

One safety note I put in the plan: the board reports `MPos:111.470,-192.628,5.000,0.000`, so that's a configured machine rather than a bare desk board. Worth confirming what it's attached to before any hardware phase runs a job.

content.text:
Fair challenge, and having actually worked through it, my original justification doesn't hold up. Let me give you the honest version.

**The reasons I gave were weak.** "ESP3D-WEBUI uses Preact so patterns transfer" is close to worthless here — we're explicitly discarding their UI, which is the only part those patterns would apply to. And "ten display pages and live status needs real state management" was asserted rather than shown.

**What the screen actually does.** I went through the re-render surface pane by pane. Four axes × four readouts is sixteen numbers, updating at 4 Hz off the board's auto-push. Machine state, feed/speed and overrides are maybe eight more fields. The offset tables are nine work offsets plus a tool table, both static until someone edits a cell. The program pane is a list with exactly one highlighted line, and the highlight is driven by `Ln:` straight out of the status report. That is a fixed set of nodes whose text changes — precisely the case where a virtual DOM's diffing earns nothing, because there is no structural churn to diff.

**The framing I missed the first time.** The classic HAAS control is a character-cell text display. Leaning into that rather than fighting it, each page becomes a pure function from state to markup, and the screen update is setting the content of a handful of panes. That gives you the same guarantee a framework's main selling point gives you — the UI is a function of state, so it cannot drift out of sync — without the framework. It also happens to be more faithful to the machine we're imitating, and the pages become directly testable: you can assert on the exact screen text a given state produces, with no DOM involved. For a teaching project that's a genuine bonus.

**The keypad argues against Preact too.** Around 120 keys, built once from a data table, with a single delegated click listener on the container. In JSX that's the same table plus a component wrapper; in plain DOM it's the table and one listener. A framework is neutral at best there, and 120 individual handlers would be worse.

**What Preact would actually buy** is fine-grained diffing we don't need and an ecosystem we won't touch. It isn't a size problem — it's about 4 KB gzipped against a 150 KB budget. The real cost is the JSX transform in the build chain and a component/hooks model that doesn't match a text-mode display.

That has a knock-on effect: with no JSX, Vite's main draw goes with it. A single `esbuild --bundle --minify` call plus roughly ten lines to inline the result into `index.html` and gzip it covers the single-file-for-SD-card requirement with fewer moving parts than Vite plus a singlefile plugin.

One thing I would not simplify away either way: g-code loaded from a file is untrusted text, so it gets escaped before it goes anywhere near markup. That's a small helper, not a framework problem, but it shouldn't get lost in the trimming.

questions.question: Given that analysis, which rendering approach should the plan commit to?

options.label: Vanilla + esbuild (Recommended)
options.description: Pages are pure state→markup functions, screen updates set pane content. Build is one esbuild call plus a short inline/gzip script. Fewest moving parts, no JSX transform, pages unit-testable without a DOM.

options.label: Keep Preact + Vite
options.description: As originally planned. Costs a JSX transform and a component/hooks model that doesn't match a text-mode display, but gives a familiar structure and a dev server with HMR out of the box.

options.label: Vanilla, but keep Vite
options.description: Same pure-function pages as the recommended option, but Vite stays for its dev server and hot reload. One extra dependency bought purely for developer convenience during the build-out.

content.text:
Found it — and page 45 of that manual restructures my plan more than the framework question does.

The 2014 control display isn't a set of full-screen pages at all. It's **one fixed layout of 13 panes** — mode bar, program display, main display, active codes, active tool, coolant, timers/tool management, alarm status, system status bar, position display, input bar, icon bar, spindle status. The mode determines which panes are populated, and the interaction rule is that **the active pane has a white background and is the only one you can enter data into**; display keys move that white highlight around. There are only three modes, not the long list I assumed: Setup (`[ZERO RETURN]`, `[HANDLE JOG]`), Edit (`[EDIT]`, `[MDI/DNC]`, `[LIST PROGRAM]`), and Operation (`[MEMORY]`), each shown in the bar as `SETUP: JOG`, `EDIT: MDI`, `OPERATION: MEM`. My phase plan was organized around building one screen page at a time, which is the wrong decomposition — the right one is to build the 13-pane shell and the active-pane mechanic first, then fill panes.

That finding also happens to settle the rendering argument harder than my earlier reasoning did: a fixed 13-pane layout where one pane is white and a few text fields update at 4 Hz is about as far from "needs a virtual DOM" as a UI gets.

Now, the options I didn't give you.

**On rendering, I skipped the middle ground.** Tagged-template renderers like `uhtml` or `lit-html` let you keep pages as pure functions returning `` html`...` `` templates, with no JSX and therefore no compile transform, while still getting real keyed DOM updates so refreshing sixteen numbers touches sixteen text nodes instead of rebuilding a pane. They also escape interpolated values by construction, which removes the g-code-into-markup hazard I flagged as something not to simplify away. That's probably a better answer than either pole I offered you. I couldn't confirm their current gzipped sizes because the search was declined, so treat "very small" as my recollection rather than a checked number. Two further options: rendering the whole display to a `<canvas>` as a character grid would be the most authentic and would let you do phosphor and scanline treatment, but it gives screen readers nothing and costs you text selection; and native custom elements are the true zero-dependency answer but add lifecycle ceremony for encapsulation this app doesn't need.

**On not writing a sender at all**, there are two real candidates. Forking gSender gets you a proven grblHAL streaming layer, but it's a large React/Electron codebase whose entire view layer you'd be replacing, and Electron fights the "serve it from the board's SD card" goal. Re-theming ESP3D-WebUI is tempting since it already runs on your board, but it's a view-layer rewrite either way, and my understanding is it's GPLv3 — which would pull aaSender into GPLv3 alongside it, when your ClearCore repo is deliberately MIT. I didn't re-verify that license, and it's worth checking before anyone invests in that path, because it's a licensing decision more than a technical one.

**The option I think most deserves your attention is the simulator.** Rather than hand-writing a virtual grblHAL, you could compile grblHAL itself to WebAssembly with a stub HAL that integrates position over time instead of driving steppers. For a teaching tool the payoff is real: students get the actual parser, the actual error and alarm codes, the actual modal handling and status formatting, so a classroom seat behaves identically to the bench machine and the entire class of "my simulator lies about the real control" bugs vanishes by construction. The costs are an emscripten toolchain, the HAL stubbing, and bundle size — a compiled grblHAL almost certainly blows the 150 KB single-file budget, so it'd load as a separate `.wasm` rather than inline. I believe grblHAL has a simulator driver and there's precedent in grbl-sim, but my search was declined so I haven't verified that. The hedge is attractive: hand-written simulator in Phase 1 to unblock everything, WASM swapped in later behind the same transport interface — which is a concrete argument for that interface existing at all.

**And one assumption worth re-examining:** my plan treats board-served as the primary deployment. For a classroom, the primary mode might really be many simulator seats served from one LAN host, with real-machine sessions occasional. If so, the size budget matters much less and the WASM simulator matters much more.

message.content: why uhtml/lit-html over other options

content.text:
The decisive reason only became clear when I read page 45, so let me start there rather than with the library comparison.

The HAAS model is that the active pane is where you type — offsets, the input bar, MDI blocks — and that data entry coexists with a status stream arriving every 250 ms. Those two things are in direct tension under naive rendering. If a status report rebuilds a pane's contents while a student is halfway through typing a work offset, the focused input is destroyed and the caret goes with it. Same for text selection: a student trying to select a line of the program listing can't hold a selection through a 4 Hz refresh. That's not a performance concern, it's a functional one, and it's the thing that actually rules out the plain-DOM approach I was advocating an hour ago.

You can work around it in plain DOM — track which pane holds focus, skip re-rendering that one, reconcile when focus leaves. But that is the beginning of writing a diffing renderer by hand, and doing it badly. A template library preserves node identity across updates as its whole job, so a re-render leaves the focused input and the selection alone and touches only the text that changed. That's the property I'm paying a dependency for, and it's the case where a dependency earns its place rather than replacing a few lines of code.

There's a smaller, more mundane benefit that will bite on ordinary files regardless of security: `innerHTML` parses whatever you interpolate. A perfectly legal g-code comment like `(SETUP: X<0 SIDE)` corrupts the pane when spliced into markup as a string. Tagged templates turn interpolations into text nodes, so that can't happen and nobody has to remember an `esc()` call at every site. I'd rather have the property than the discipline.

**Against Preact the argument is much weaker, and I want to be straight about that.** Preact solves both of those problems equally well — it also escapes, and it also preserves identity. The difference is not correctness. It's that JSX needs a compile transform, which is the reason Vite was in the plan at all; tagged templates are ordinary JavaScript and run from plain ES modules, so the build collapses to bundle-and-minify. Preact is also somewhat larger, though I couldn't check current numbers since the search was declined. If you or anyone else who'll touch this is more fluent in JSX, that fluency is worth more than the build-chain saving, and Preact is a perfectly defensible choice. I'm not going to pretend that one is close.

**Against canvas**, the interesting thing is that it also dodges the re-render problem, since you simply redraw. What kills it is that you'd hand-roll text layout, caret rendering, and hit-testing for roughly 120 keys and 13 panes, and you'd hand back all accessibility and text selection. And the main thing canvas is usually reached for here — the CRT look, phosphor glow, scanlines — is available with CSS over ordinary DOM via `text-shadow` and an overlay. So it costs a great deal and buys an aesthetic you can get anyway.

Two caveats. Between the two libraries, `lit-html` is the conservative pick — widely used and Google-maintained — while `uhtml` is smaller but a much smaller project; for something meant to outlive this term, maintenance probably matters more than a couple of kilobytes. And I should flag that this is my third position on the question: Preact, then plain DOM, now this. The first change was me correcting a badly-argued default. The second came from the manual telling me the display has live data entry inside it, which is a fact I didn't have before and which genuinely changes the answer.

content.text:
Fair question, and answering it properly means first correcting something I got wrong in my own argument.

**I strawmanned plain DOM.** My case against it assumed you'd rebuild each pane's contents wholesale on every status report, which is what breaks focus and selection. But that's a choice, not a requirement. The alternative is to build the DOM once, hold references to the roughly 25 text nodes that actually change, and assign `textContent` to them — surgical updates. That preserves focus and selection by construction because you never touch the input's node, sidesteps the escaping issue entirely because `textContent` doesn't parse markup, and is the fastest option available. The real cost isn't correctness, it's that the state-to-node mapping is manual, so it can drift out of sync as the app grows across six phases. That's a maintainability argument, which is much more honest than the correctness argument I made.

On the frameworks you're asking about. **Vue** would work fine and solves the same problems Preact does. Its fine-grained reactivity is a genuinely nice fit for a DRO — you'd hold position as a ref and bindings update without re-running a render function. But Vue's strengths are aimed at app-shaped applications with many distinct views, routing, and stores, and this is one fixed screen with 13 panes. It's also the heaviest of the serious candidates. Not wrong, just carrying weight it won't use. **Svelte** is arguably the best technical fit of anything mentioned: the compiler turns your markup into direct DOM assignments, so updating 16 numbers emits 16 surgical writes with essentially no runtime framework in the bundle, and it handles focus and identity correctly. The cost is a compiler in the build and a syntax to learn. **Solid** gets you the same surgical updates via signals with a very small runtime, but wants a JSX transform. **Lit** — the full library rather than bare lit-html — gives you reactive custom elements, which is the standards-native answer and would let panes be genuine `<haas-pane>` elements. **Alpine or petite-vue** are aimed at sprinkling reactivity onto existing HTML rather than being the architecture of an app like this, and **van.js** is interesting as a roughly 1 KB reactive layer if minimalism is the goal.

Here's the thing I should say plainly rather than bury: **at this workload, performance does not distinguish any of them.** Twenty-five values at 4 Hz and one list with a moving highlight is trivial for every option on that list, including the manual one. Anyone who tells you a virtual DOM is too slow here, or that signals are necessary, is arguing about nothing. So the honest criteria are how much build machinery you're taking on, how big the bundle gets if you're serving it off the SD card, and — the one that probably dominates — what you and any future contributor already know.

That last point deserves weight. For a project this size, on a six-phase build where the hard parts are the HAAS workflow semantics and the g-code streaming rather than the rendering, your existing fluency is worth more than any marginal technical fit among these. If you're already fluent in Vue, use Vue; the time you'd lose learning Lit's idioms is real and the technical difference is not.

So: is uhtml/lit-html the best option based on this conversation? I'd put it this way. Lit is my recommendation *if you have no strong existing preference*, because it's small, needs no compile transform, is standards-adjacent, is well maintained, and matches a fixed-pane text display without ceremony. Svelte is the strongest purely technical fit if you don't mind the compiler. Surgical vanilla is entirely viable and I shouldn't have dismissed it the way I did. And Vue, Preact, or Solid are all defensible, with the choice among them coming down to familiarity rather than fit.

What I'd push back on is only the two extremes: canvas, which costs accessibility and text selection to buy a look CSS can give you, and rebuilding panes with `innerHTML`, which is the one approach that genuinely breaks the data-entry model the manual describes.

The plan file still says Preact, and I'll leave it there until you tell me which way you want to go.

# aaSender — a HAAS-lookalike g-code sender for grblHAL / ClearCore

## Context

`/home/holla/aaSender` holds two photos of a HAAS mill pendant (`images/haas1.jpg`,
`images/haas2.jpg`) and the 2014 Mill Operator's Manual (96-8200, 404 pp) in
`reference/`. The goal is a browser-based g-code sender whose entire operator
interface replicates that pendant, so students learning on HAAS machines can
practice the real workflow — modes, display panes, HANDLE JOG, CYCLE START,
offsets, on-control editing — against a hobby-class grblHAL machine or nothing at all.

The target hardware is the companion project **`/home/holla/grblhal-clearcore`**
(Teknic ClearCore, SAME53, bare-metal grblHAL, 4-axis XYZA), already bench-verified
with Ethernet, telnet, WebSocket, HTTP, the WebUI plugin, SD job streaming and USB
CDC. It currently serves ESP3D-WebUI v3 from SD `/www`. aaSender is the
HAAS-skinned replacement for that UI.

**Decisions made with the user:**
- Three transports: network WebSocket, Web Serial over USB, and a built-in
  simulator so a classroom seat needs no hardware.
- Full pendant replica — clickable keypad and screen, operated like a real HAAS.
- Scope: operator essentials **plus** programming — EDIT mode, MDI, offset entry.
- Rendering with **Lit** (see the reasoning section).

---

## Verified against the live board

The ClearCore was powered up at `192.168.0.113` during planning, so the transport
design is **measured, not assumed**. Open ports: 23 (telnet), 80 (HTTP), 81 (WebSocket).

```
$I  → [VER:1.1f.20260726:] [OPT:VNML,100,1024,4,0] [AXS:4:XYZA]
      [NEWOPT:ENUMS,RT+,TC,SED,ETH,FS,SD] [FIRMWARE:grblHAL]
?   → <Idle|MPos:111.470,-192.628,5.000,0.000|Bf:100,1023|Ln:187756|FS:0,0|Ov:100,100,100>
$#  → [G54:…] … [G59.3:…] [G28:…] [G30:…] [G92:…]
      [TLO:0.000,0.000,0.000,0.000]  [PRB:0.000,0.000,0.000,0.000:0]
$G  → [GC:G1 G54 G17 G21 G90 G94 G49 G98 G50 M5 M9 T0 F2540 S0.]
$13 → 0   (millimetres)
```

**The load-bearing finding:** the WebSocket carries the grbl stream **only when the
client negotiates the `webui-v3` subprotocol.** With no subprotocol, or with
`arduino`, the handshake completes and then nothing passes in either direction —
verified with both text and binary frames. With `webui-v3` the socket is fully
bidirectional: `$I` sent over it returned its reply over it.

| Measured | Consequence |
|---|---|
| `webui-v3` required for any data flow | The network transport must request that subprotocol. Not optional. |
| Two text frames on connect: `currentID:<n>`, `activeID:<n>` | ESP3D session handshake — filter before the grbl parser. |
| Reports auto-push every 250 ms (`$397=250` already set) | Don't blindly poll `?`. Poll only after ~500 ms of silence; self-tunes across all transports. |
| `Ln:187756` present | Running line number comes free — no sender-side tracking needed. |
| `[OPT:…,100,1024,…]`, `Bf:100,1023` | Planner 100 blocks, RX buffer **1024**, not the classic 128. |
| `[AXS:4:XYZA]` | Position and offset panes are 4-axis. |
| Nine coordinate systems reported (through `G59.3`) | `G59.1`–`G59.3` can back HAAS `G154 P1`–`P3`. |
| `[TLO:0,0,0,0]` | TLO is per-axis, not a scalar. |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on all HTTP responses | No CORS problem even from a laptop dev server. |
| `GET /command?cmd=…` returns only `ok`; output goes to the socket | HTTP is a command sink. Since the socket also accepts writes, **ignore HTTP for commands entirely.** |
| `GET /` serves 93,373 bytes gzipped from SD `/www` | aaSender installs the same way and should fit a comparable budget. |
| `N_TOOLS 0` in `src/grbl/config.h` | Board has **no tool table** — the sender must own it. |
| Repo MIT; grblHAL core GPLv3 | aaSender links no grblHAL code, so MIT is fine. |

Worth reporting to the companion project: a conventional sender (ioSender, gSender)
connecting over WebSocket without `webui-v3` sees a dead socket with no diagnostic.
Out of scope here — aaSender simply negotiates `webui-v3`.

---

## What the control actually looks like

From the 2014 manual (PDF page = printed page + 20). Key pages: **PDF 55** — figure
F2.26, the full keyboard with all eight groups labelled; **PDF 65** — figure F2.27,
the display layout with thirteen numbered callouts; **PDF 66** — the mode bar and
mode table. This is the *late-classic* control, which is what `images/haas1.jpg`
shows — not the older full-screen green display.

**The display is one fixed layout of 13 panes**, not a set of full-screen pages:

```
 1 Mode and Active Display Bar      8 Alarm Status
 2 Program Display                  9 System Status Bar
 3 Main Display                    10 Position Display / Axis Load Meters
 4 Active Codes                    11 Input Bar
 5 Active Tool                     12 Icon Bar
 6 Coolant                         13 Spindle Status / Editor Help
 7 Timers, Counters / Tool Management
```

Two rules drive the whole interaction model, and they are the thing to get right:

- **The active pane has a white background, and it is the only pane you can enter
  data into.** Display keys move that highlight. Everything else is read-only.
- **There are three modes, not a long list.** Setup (`[ZERO RETURN]`,
  `[HANDLE JOG]`), Edit (`[EDIT]`, `[MDI/DNC]`, `[LIST PROGRAM]`), Operation
  (`[MEMORY]`). The bar shows `SETUP: JOG`, `EDIT: MDI`, `OPERATION: MEM` on the
  left and the current display function on the right.

**The keyboard has eight groups** (F2.26): Function, Cursor, Display, Mode, Numeric,
Alpha, Jog, Overrides. The manual's artwork is vector, so
`pdftoppm -f 55 -l 55 -r 600 -png` gives clean reference art at any size.

---

## Rendering: Lit

Not an obvious call, and the reasoning is worth recording because it reversed twice.

The display is a fixed 13-pane layout where roughly 25 scalar fields update at 4 Hz
and one list carries a moving highlight. **Performance does not distinguish any
candidate at this scale** — Lit, Preact, Vue, Svelte, Solid and hand-written DOM are
all far more than fast enough. So the decision rests on build machinery, bundle
size, and fit.

What rules out the naive approach is the active-pane model: data entry happens
*inside* a display that refreshes four times a second. Replacing a pane's contents
with `innerHTML` on each status report destroys the focused input, the caret, and
any text selection — exactly while a student is typing a work offset. Preserving
node identity across updates is therefore a correctness requirement, not an
optimisation. Lit does that as its whole job, and escapes interpolated values by
construction, which also stops a legal g-code comment like `(SETUP: X<0 SIDE)` from
corrupting a pane.

Lit specifically, over the alternatives: it needs **no compile transform** (tagged
templates are ordinary JavaScript), so the build collapses to bundle-and-minify; it
is small, well-maintained, and standards-adjacent, so panes can be real custom
elements. Svelte is the strongest purely technical fit but adds a compiler; Preact,
Vue and Solid are all defensible and would come down to familiarity; canvas would
cost accessibility and text selection to buy a look CSS can give with `text-shadow`
and an overlay. Hand-written surgical DOM updates are genuinely viable too — the
reason to prefer Lit is that the manual state-to-node mapping drifts as the app
grows across six phases, not that it would be slow or incorrect.

**Build:** `esbuild --bundle --minify`, then a short script to inline the result into
`index.html` and gzip it. No JSX means no Vite; add Vite later only if a dev server
with hot reload earns its keep. `python3 -m http.server` on localhost is a secure
context, so Web Serial works in development without HTTPS.

**Size budget:** ESP3D-WebUI is 91 KB gzipped, so **≤150 KB gzipped**, enforced by a
build-script check that fails loudly when exceeded.

---

## Layout

```
index.html
build.js           esbuild + inline + gzip, with the size check
src/
  main.js
  grbl.js          status/ok/error/alarm parsing, error+alarm tables,
                   character-counting job streamer
  transport.js     one interface, three impls: WebSocket | Web Serial | Simulator
  sim.js           virtual grblHAL machine
  haas.js          machine model: modes, work/tool offsets, timers,
                   grbl -> HAAS alarm mapping
  keys.js          the eight key groups from F2.26, key -> action dispatch
  ui/pendant.js    bezel, logo, E-stop, handle-jog dial, keypad
  ui/screen.js     the 13-pane shell, mode bar, active-pane routing
  ui/panes/*.js    one file per numbered pane in F2.27
  haas.css         palette and pendant chrome
test/grbl.test.js  node --test: streamer flow control + status parsing
reference/         2014 Mill Operator's Manual (96-8200)
```

One file per numbered pane, because the manual numbers them and a student will look
them up that way. Everything else stays collapsed until it earns a split.

### Transport interface

```js
{ connect(), send(str), sendRealtime(byte), onLine(cb), disconnect() }
```

- **WebSocket** — `new WebSocket("ws://<ip>:81/", ["webui-v3"])`, `binaryType =
  "arraybuffer"`, decode with `TextDecoder`, drop the `currentID:` / `activeID:`
  handshake lines, split the rest on `\n`. Writes go over the same socket.
- **Web Serial** — `navigator.serial.requestPort()`, 115200 8N1,
  `TextDecoderStream` split on `\n`. Needs a secure context (localhost or HTTPS);
  Chrome/Edge only. The board enumerates as `2890:8022`.
- **Simulator** — same interface, no I/O.

Status acquisition is uniform: if no `<…>` report has arrived for 500 ms, send `?`.
On the ClearCore's auto-push that timer never fires; on serial it becomes a 5 Hz
poll. One rule, three transports.

### Job streaming

The one piece of genuinely non-trivial logic. Character-counting flow control: keep
a queue of the byte lengths of lines sent but not acknowledged; send the next line
only while `sum(pending) + len(next) < rxBuffer`; pop the oldest length on each `ok`
or `error:N`; halt the stream and raise an alarm on `error:N`.

`rxBuffer` is a **calibration knob seeded from the board** — default 128, raised to
the value parsed from `[OPT:…]` / `Bf:` at connect (1024 here). Never a hardcoded
constant.

This gets the project's one required test (`test/grbl.test.js`, `node --test`): feed
a scripted line list plus acks, assert in-flight bytes never exceed the buffer and
every line is sent exactly once.

### Simulator

A JS virtual grblHAL speaking the same wire protocol: `ok` per accepted line,
`<Idle|MPos:…|Bf:…|Ln:…|FS:…>` on `?` and on a 250 ms auto-push, honouring `!` / `~`
/ `0x18` and the override bytes, walking position along each move at the programmed
feedrate, with a way to force a limit alarm so students see the alarm pane work.

No acceleration planner and no lookahead — position is linearly interpolated per
move. Marked with a `ponytail:` comment naming that ceiling.

**Deliberate upgrade path:** compiling grblHAL itself to WebAssembly with a stub HAL
would give students the real parser, real error and alarm codes, and real modal
handling, so a classroom seat behaves identically to the bench machine. That is
strictly better but costs an emscripten toolchain and blows the single-file size
budget, so it loads separately if pursued. The transport interface makes it a
drop-in replacement later — which is much of why that interface exists.

---

## HAAS → grblHAL mapping

Belongs in the repo README too. Real-time byte values from the Grbl v1.1 interface docs.

| HAAS pendant control | grbl / grblHAL |
|---|---|
| CYCLE START | `~` (0x7E), or start the streamer |
| FEED HOLD | `!` (0x21) |
| RESET | soft reset 0x18 |
| EMERGENCY STOP | 0x18 + stop streaming (real E-stop is hardware — say so in HELP) |
| FEEDRATE 100% / +10% / −10% | 0x90 / 0x91 / 0x92 |
| SPINDLE 100% / +10% / −10% | 0x99 / 0x9A / 0x9B |
| RAPID 100% / 50% / 25% | 0x95 / 0x96 / 0x97 |
| RAPID 5% | **no grbl equivalent** — see gaps |
| COOLANT | flood toggle 0xA0 |
| SPINDLE CW / CCW / STOP | `M3` / `M4` / `M5` (0x9E only acts in HOLD) |
| HANDLE JOG + increment | `$J=G91 F<rate> X<inc>`; jog cancel 0x85 |
| ZERO RETURN → ALL | `$H` |
| ZERO RETURN → HOME G28 | `G28` |
| Position: MACHINE | `MPos:` |
| Position: WORK G54 | `MPos − WCO` |
| Position: DIST TO GO | computed from the running block's target |
| Position: OPERATOR | sender-side zeroable display |
| Program display highlight | `Ln:` — confirmed present |
| OFFSET → WORK G54–G59 | `G10 L2 P1..6`, read back with `$#` |
| OFFSET → WORK G154 P1–P3 | `G59.1` / `G59.2` / `G59.3` |
| OFFSET → TOOL length | sender-owned tool table, emitted as `G43.1 Z−<offset>` |
| Alarm status pane | `ALARM:N` / `error:N`, shown with grbl code *and* HAAS-style text |
| Active Codes pane | `$G` modal string |
| MDI | typed block sent directly |
| LIST PROGRAM | programs stored by O-number in browser storage |
| TOOL OFFSET MEASURE / PART ZERO SET | write into the sender's tables, then `G10 L2` |

### Gaps to design around, not paper over

- **RAPID 5%** does not exist in grbl (only 100/50/25). Render the key and have it
  post "not supported on this control" rather than silently lying.
- **Tool table**: `N_TOOLS 0`, and base GRBL has only dynamic TLO. aaSender owns the
